title: Value first: the hook speaks the viewer's language and the value lands by beat two
when: When ordering the beats of any narrated, story-driven video (explainer, documentary, product or case story).
summary: Lead with why it is valuable, not with what it is or how it was made (a reverse iceberg). The first beat answers 'why should I care' in outcome language: what the viewer gains, avoids or finally understands. The value claim lands by the second beat; everything after it is evidence in service of that claim. Numbers belong in the hook only when they carry stakes, never as inventory.
steps: Write the one-line message: 'This video tells [audience] that [message].'
Put the value claim in beat 1 or beat 2.
Order the remaining beats as evidence for the claim (mechanism, example, proof).
Self-check: delete the evidence beats; the value beats must still state the value. Delete the value beats; if the video still seems to work, it was a feature tour, not a story.
do: Present the plan as a proposal: each scene with its beat, what is on screen and WHY, traced back to the message.
Mine the source's own entities, numbers and metaphors for the visuals before inventing generic props.
avoid: Subject-internal vocabulary in the hook (file names, feature lists, the source article's headings).
A scene whose 'why' cannot be traced to the message; cut it rather than decorate it.
Props that could appear unchanged in another subject's video.
checks: The value claim is stated by the second beat.
Every scene's why traces to the one-line message.

title: Choose one explainer structure and extract the teaching truth first
when: When turning a topic, an article or evidence into an explainer or documentary script.
summary: An article is an information dump; a video is a guided act of understanding. Never paraphrase the source in its own order. First extract the teaching truth (audience, gap or stakes, the one-line thesis, a 3-6 idea spine, the evidence, the landing), then pick ONE structure: concept explainer, how-to process, listicle or story explainer.
steps: Extract: audience and what they already know; the gap or stakes; the thesis in one line; the 3-6 ideas that build to it; the concrete evidence; the landing (takeaway or call to think, try or act).
Concept explainer ('what is X and why it matters'): name the concept, reveal the mechanism layer by layer, land the implication.
How-to process: 3-6 ordered steps on one consistent visual stage, one move each.
Listicle ('N things about X'): hook, N roughly equal items, wrap; three is the strongest count.
Story explainer: setup, tension, turn, resolution, lesson; the lesson generalises.
Build the body as a sequence of 3-6 scenes that build understanding cumulatively, not one isolated scene.
avoid: Following the source's paragraph order (the most common failure).
Scenes whose only job is 'more detail' or 'another point'.
checks: One structure is named.
Each scene has one job and a one-sentence key message.

title: Pick the hook strategy from the idea, and vary it
when: When choosing how an explainer or story opens.
summary: Nine opening strategies each fit a different situation: a shocking statistic (a credible number quantifies the stakes), a rhetorical question (an immediate gap), a counterintuitive claim (the truth contradicts belief), pain validation (the audience already feels the confusion), a visceral metaphor (an abstract idea made concrete), a concept announcement (the term itself is the subject), direct address (a clearly defined audience), imagine-a-scenario (a thought experiment frames the piece) and stakes or consequence (a real cost of getting it wrong).
do: Name the strategy for every opening.
Rotate strategies across a channel; do not open every video with a statistic.
avoid: A generic opening such as 'Welcome to…' or 'Introducing…'; if the first line is generic, start over.
checks: The opening line creates tension, curiosity or surprise within the first 3 seconds.
source: HyperFrames faceless-explainer story-design.md (hook strategy table) and hyperframes-creative narration.md (Apache-2.0, 6308727), restated

title: Give every scene a named clarity technique
when: When planning what each scene does to make an idea understood.
summary: 'Explain the idea' is not a technique. Each scene names one from six families: make it concrete (analogy, concretisation, a worked example with real numbers, anchoring on something familiar); reveal in order (progressive disclosure, build-up from simple to general, signposting); contrast (before/after, belief vs reality, two options, a counterexample); structure (rule of three, numbered list, question then answer, frame then fill); evidence (statistic, citation, demonstration, causal chain A to B to C); memory and landing (callback to the hook's image, one-line distillation, a coined term, generalisation).
do: Match the technique to the graphic: a contrast to a comparison, a causal chain to a flow diagram, a worked example to a chart, a numbered list to a list build.
avoid: A scene with no technique beyond restating the narration.
checks: Every scene's plan names its clarity technique.
source: HyperFrames faceless-explainer story-design.md (clarity/rhetoric technique catalog, Apache-2.0, 6308727), restated

title: Ride a comprehension arc: open the gap, orient, build, land
when: When assigning the intended feeling of each scene in an explainer or documentary.
summary: Each scene names a specific target feeling, not 'positive' or 'interested'. The arc runs: a negative valley that opens the gap (curiosity, puzzlement, surprise, tension, skepticism, recognition); a pivot that orients (clarity, anticipation, focus); a build that grows understanding (comprehension, 'aha', confidence, fascination, momentum, conviction, unease for a caveat); and a resolution that lands (satisfaction, resolve, inspiration, 'now I get it'). Compound beats such as 'surprise and recognition' are often strongest.
do: Vary the beats across the video so the arc moves.
Let the beat drive pacing and transitions: a valley holds, a build moves.
avoid: The same beat on every scene.
checks: The beat list shows a valley, a pivot, a build and a resolution.
source: HyperFrames faceless-explainer story-design.md (emotional beats, Apache-2.0, 6308727), restated

title: Write narration to be spoken: pace, spoken numbers and revealable cues
when: When writing or reviewing narration that a TTS voice will read.
summary: TTS reads literally, so write numbers the way they should be said ('nearly two trillion dollars', 'ten times', 'A P I') while the screen shows the exact figure. Natural pace is about 2.5 words a second and the script should feel shorter than the video: silence between sentences is a feature. Write each line as discrete phrases with clear boundaries so the on-screen pieces can appear when the voice names them.
steps: Size the script at about 2.5 words per second (150 a minute), then trim to leave breathing room.
Spell out symbols, abbreviations and big numbers as they should sound.
Use contractions and vary sentence length; read it aloud.
Split long clauses into phrases ('first the snowball, then the hill, then the speed') so reveals can land on each.
avoid: Brochure phrases ('unlock the power of', 'seamless experience').
Long noun-phrase lists.
Run-on sentences a graphic cannot pace to.
checks: No raw symbols or digit strings the voice would misread remain in the narration text.
source: HyperFrames hyperframes-creative/references/narration.md and faceless-explainer story-design.md script rules (Apache-2.0, 6308727), restated

title: Smooth beats bouncy: long-tail settles, overshoot only when playful
when: Whenever a graphic, text or element animates in.
summary: Elements settle on a long-tail deceleration (power3-like, or expo-out on a fast arrival). Bounce, back-out and elastic eases are the most common instant turn-off in generated videos: they buy emphasis at the cost of cleanliness. Overshoot is a rare, explicitly playful exception, never the house style. The canvas templates in this program follow this rule.
avoid: back-out, bounce or elastic as a default entrance.
Hand-keyed overshoot.
checks: No default entrance overshoots its final position.
source: HyperFrames faceless-explainer/references/motion-language.md part 2 rule 1 (Apache-2.0, 6308727); applied in motion-templates.js

title: Reveal each element when the voice names it, across the later half
when: When a graphic shows several items (list entries, chart bars, steps, comparison sides).
summary: Dumping everything on screen in the first quarter of a scene is what makes a video feel like a slideshow. Bring on only what the voice is saying at the start; reveal every further piece on its spoken cue, spreading reveals across the later ~50% of the scene. Fewer things on screen, each arriving on its beat, beat a full canvas that animated once and froze.
steps: Find the spoken moment of each item in the narration.
Start each item's entrance at its cue, not on a fixed stagger.
Hold the finished graphic after the last cue.
avoid: All elements entering at once.
Content entering and then freezing for the rest of the scene.

numbers.front_load_limit: nothing beyond what is spoken in the first ~25% of the scene

checks: Each revealed item appears within a beat of the narration naming it.

title: No motion over bad motion: no breathing loops, no back-half drift on graphics
when: When a designed graphic or text card holds on screen.
summary: Two reflexive ways of faking life read cheap: scaling cards up and down in a loop ('breathing'), and a slow pan or push on graphic elements in the later half of a scene, which pulls the viewer's eye off what it was reading. A held, still graphic is better. The only sanctioned aliveness is a subtle, low-amplitude jitter or the subject itself doing something. This rule is for designed graphics; documentary photographs keep their purposeful camera moves (editing.still-image-motion).
avoid: Looping scale 'breathing' on cards or text.
A slow pan or push over graphic elements in the back half of a scene.
Many elements floating independently as 'motion'.
do: Hold still after the last reveal; use subtle jitter only if the hold feels dead.
checks: No graphic loops its scale; no graphic drifts after its last reveal.

title: Cut the curve: seams cut at peak velocity with matched direction
when: When two moving elements or two moving shots meet at a cut.
summary: A static cut between moving scenes feels like a slideshow. Let the outgoing hero accelerate in one direction, cut mid-motion, and let the incoming hero continue in the same direction and decelerate, using mirrored eases with the same distance and duration so the speed matches at the cut. Nothing needs to travel fully off screen: partial travel plus an early fade carries the eye.
steps: Pick one direction for the seam; both sides move that way.
Exit on an accelerating curve, enter on the mirrored decelerating curve, same distance and duration.
Keep the exit short (0.2-0.4 s); the entry is at least as long.
Fade the exit out by about a quarter of its travel; the last fading element dies right at the cut.
avoid: Elements on different paths across a cut.
A gentle entry ease after a fast exit.
Full off-screen travel.
Dead air: nothing moving at the seam.
checks: Neighbouring camera moves at a cut share direction, or the cut is a deliberate contrast.

title: Body sequences share one stage and one seam; vary framings across the video
when: When planning how consecutive body scenes look and connect.
summary: A run of body scenes reads as one flow when they share a consistent stage (the same diagram growing, the same number line) and repeat one seam type. When one element transforms into another, keep the transform inside one scene rather than splitting it across a cut. Across the whole video use at least three different framings (centred hero, rule of thirds, split screen, layered depth, asymmetric 60/40, triptych, full-width strip) and never the same framing twice in a row. Use two or three transition types for the whole video.
avoid: The same framing on two consecutive scenes.
A different transition type at every seam.
checks: At least three framings appear; no framing repeats back to back.
source: HyperFrames faceless-explainer story-design.md (continuity, transitions) and visual-design.md (layout, Apache-2.0, 6308727), restated

title: Keep graphics out of the caption band
when: Whenever a video carries burned-in captions, and for bottom-edge consistency even when it does not.
summary: The bottom ~17% of the frame belongs to captions. Plan primary content and key visuals into the top ~83%, and anchor a centred hero at about 0.42 of the height rather than the exact middle. Background and full-bleed footage are exempt.
avoid: Lower-third graphics, chart labels or list text inside the caption band while captions are on.
checks: No graphic text block extends into the bottom 17% while captions are shown.

title: Captions are a clean rail; emphasis is inline and scarce
when: When styling burned-in captions for narration.
summary: The caption rail carries the whole narration verbatim: a readable lower-third subtitle, one group on screen at a time, at most two lines, broken at clause boundaries, with a short fade in and out. Its only intensity is an inline emphasis on the one or two punch words of a phrase (accent colour or a small active-word lift). Big, effect-heavy captions are a scarce peak, not the default. Legibility comes from a tight shadow or box local to the text, never from grading the picture.
steps: Size about 4.5% of the frame height; one clean sans at weight 500-600; white or near white.
At most two lines of about 32-42 characters, broken at a clause, never leaving one dangling word.
Each group stays at least 0.5 s; fade in and out over 150-250 ms.
Mark at most one or two emphasis words per group, inline.
Drop only filler (um, uh, exact stutters); never drop content to fit fewer groups.
avoid: Accumulating captions into a multi-line poem.
Per-word choreography on every word.
Bare light text on bright backgrounds.
checks: Every narration word appears exactly once in the captions.
No two caption groups are on screen together.
source: HyperFrames skills/embedded-captions/references/rail.md and SKILL.md caption model (Apache-2.0, 6308727), restated

title: Group caption words by pauses, sentence ends, density and limits
when: When turning word timings into caption groups.
summary: Close a group at a real pause or at the end of a sentence or clause, and cap its size by how fast the words come: dense speech gets shorter groups. Each group appears just before its first word and leaves shortly after its last, never overlapping the next.
steps: Close the group after a pause of 0.18 s or more, or after a word ending in . ? ! , ; : or a dash.
Cap words per group by density: more than 3.5 words a second allows 2; more than 2.5 allows 3; otherwise 4; a slow horizontal read may reach 6 words within 2.5 s.
Start the group 0.08 s before its first word.
End it at the last word plus a short tail (0.12-0.6 s), clamped to 0.05 s before the next group.
Merge a group shorter than 0.5 s or with a single word into its neighbour when the limits allow.
checks: Groups never overlap.
Every group stays on screen at least 0.5 s unless the narration itself is shorter.

title: Carve room for the voice in the music; do not just duck the whole bed
when: Whenever music plays under narration. Skip only when there is no voice for the music to sit under.
summary: Ducking the whole bed makes the music go limp for the entire narration. The voice only needs the bands it occupies (roughly 250 Hz-2.5 kHz). Cut those bands in the music, following the voice's own level so the bed comes back between phrases, and add a level match that releases slowly so the music never snaps back like a machine. The carve lives on the music track and listens to the narration; never carve a voice.
steps: Measure where the narration's energy sits and how far the bed sits above it.
Cut the bed in up to six bands between 250 Hz and 2.5 kHz, deepest where masking hurts most (around 1.6 kHz).
Drive the cuts and a gain stage from the voice's level so silence leaves the bed alone.
Release the gain slowly after each phrase.
Put any limiter last, as the ceiling.
avoid: A static carve that thins the bed through pauses.
Carving a voice track or a group that contains music or SFX.
A whole-bed duck as the finished mix.
checks: The voice is legible without the bed sounding hollow, and the bed rises between phrases.
source: HyperFrames skills/hyperframes-audio/SKILL.md and packages/core/src/audioCarve.ts carveProfile (Apache-2.0, 6308727), restated

title: Mix by relationship and symptom: subtract, level, relate, then ceiling
when: When narration or music sounds wrong, or before finishing any mix.
summary: A mix is a set of relationships, not a stack of processors. Name the symptom, then reach for its fix: hum or thump, a high-pass near 80 Hz; boomy, tame around 200 Hz; muffled, reduce mud near 250 Hz; words hard to follow, add clarity near 3 kHz or carve the bed; harsh, soften near 3.2 kHz; uneven words, gentle compression; voice and music fighting, a voiceover carve, not EQ on either. Order: subtract before adding, level after filtering, relationships after level, character and ceiling last. Diagnose by comparing within the same file (the pauses show the channel), never against a generic voice spectrum.
avoid: Diagnosing one unknown voice from its absolute spectrum.
Reverb or delay on the narration in an explainer.
Turning one track down as the reflex fix.
checks: Each processing step names the symptom it fixes.

title: Animated graphics must render identically every time
when: When building or changing any frame-drawn motion template.
summary: A frame is drawn by seeking a paused timeline to an exact time, so anything that depends on a clock, randomness or an endless loop breaks the render. Every motion is a finite function of the frame time; variation comes from the element index or a seeded generator; every entrance states its starting state explicitly.
avoid: Math.random, Date.now or wall-clock timers in a template.
Infinite or repeating loops.
CSS transitions or keyframe animations driving motion.
Relying on a hidden starting state instead of an explicit one.
do: Seed any hand-drawn wobble from the element and frame.
Prove determinism by rendering the same frame twice and comparing bytes.
checks: The same input renders byte-identical frames twice.
source: HyperFrames faceless-explainer motion-language.md part 3 and hyperframes-core determinism-rules.md (Apache-2.0, 6308727); motion.js inspectBrowser checks it
